messages.subject: ZIP / population trends
parts:
Hello, 

I am modeling bird trends using N-mixture models. Some key aspects of the data are:  ~ 80 species; ~20 years; fixed distance point counts with 1-4 reps/season; ~2800 sites; lots of NA's in data due to sites being surveyed an average of 5 (of 20) years and number of reps being variable (average of 2). I am trying it in Unmarked with the pcount function. 

For the 10 species I've explored so far, ZIP models typically have lower AIC values versus P models. Trend estimates are typically slightly different in magnitude (direction is always the same so far). It's my understanding I can't include covariates on psi (the zero-inflation parameter) in Unmarked. I might ultimately run these models using JAGS, but I have so many species, I feel a little daunted by the amount of time that could take. 

I have a few questions:
1) What is the meaning of a psi parameter when there are no covariates on it? Will it function to equally exclude bad sites (where the species isn't) as good sites (where the species is)? 
2) Are ZIP models a reasonable thing to consider when the goal is trend estimates? I imagine yes if the data generating process includes a component that's generating zeros unexplained by the component generating counts, but I haven't been able to find precedence for this (in a short search).
3) And, more broadly, are N-mixture models the way to go with these data?

Thank you in advance for any advice and help,

Valerie

messages.author: 6ad895aa93bfdc63
messages.subject: Re: ZIP / population trends
parts:
Hi Valerie,

Quick responses in italics below.
1) What is the meaning of a psi parameter when there are no covariates on it? Will it function to equally exclude bad sites (where the species isn't) as good sites (where the species is)?

Psi is a zero-inflation parameter in this context: the proportion of sites that are (excess) zero's beyond the Poisson part of the model. If the estimate of lambda is large enough that N = 0 | N~P(lambda) is nearly impossible, than this parameter approximates a probability of absence. Otherwise, zeroes can arise as either the zero inflation or the Poisson parts of the model, and I don't know that psi has any clear biological interpretation (maybe somebody else has a good interpretation). I think it would be possible to code something up that gets at whether N = 0 at a given site is arising from the ZI vs. P parts, but I don't think any such function is built-in, and again, not clear to me how to meaningfully interpret this.

2) Are ZIP models a reasonable thing to consider when the goal is trend estimates? I imagine yes if the data generating process includes a component that's generating zeros unexplained by the component generating counts, but I haven't been able to find precedence for this (in a short search).

I'm guessing that you are 'stacking' the data for analysis (i.e., year is a covariate in the model, and a 'site' in the unmarked frame really describes some site during a given year). Maybe worth noting that psi is a constant as implemented in unmarked (I think?).  An off-the-top-of head thought is that there is some risk is that the latent zero inflation across 'sites'  (site x year) could easily be more heavily allocated to some years than others. This may not be desirable. Might make more sense to construct a model where the yearly structure is explicit, which might expedite comparison of different formulations, e.g.:
z[i, t]~Bern(psi)
N[i,t] ~ P([1-z[i,t]]*lambda[i,t])
vs. 
z[i, t]~Bern(psi[t])
N[i,t] ~ P([1-z[i,t]]*lambda[i,t])
vs. 
whatever else--like an open model to capture site-specific dynamics following N[i,t]~P(exp(r)*N[i, t-1]), etc. Doesn't necessarily need to be coded in BUGS fashion.

Cheers,

John

messages.subject: Re: ZIP / population trends
parts:
Maybe more clear (in case somebody else find this down the road) and consistent with the implementation in unmarked to instead write the pseudocode above like:

z[i, t]~Bern(1-psi)
N[i,t] ~ P([z[i,t]]*lambda[i,t])
vs. 
z[i, t]~Bern(1-psi[t])
N[i,t] ~ P([z[i,t]]*lambda[i,t])
